Building an Interactive Paraglider Simulator: From Physical Sensors to Unity

An end-to-end engineering project combining mechanical prototyping, STM32 sensor acquisition, Bluetooth communication and an interactive flight simulator.

How can a pilot's real movements become responsive controls in a virtual environment? In this fifth-year engineering project, our team upgraded an existing paraglider simulator prototype to detect left and right brake inputs and weight shifting in the harness, then use those signals to control a game developed in Unity.

Engineering objective

Develop a reliable path from physical movements to digital flight commands, while making the simulator more robust, intuitive and engaging.

STM32Sensor acquisition and processing
HC-05Wireless serial communication
3 levelsProgressive Unity challenges

Starting from an existing mechanical prototype

The project inherited a wooden support structure, suspension lines, brake handles, a harness and part of the original sensor system. Our work focused on improving the mechanics and electronics, replacing the previous accelerometer-based weight-shift measurement, and completing the embedded-to-PC integration.

Designing and manufacturing the encoder mounts

Two rotary encoders measure how far the pilot pulls the brake handles. A missing encoder wheel had to be recreated, and dedicated mounts were required to secure the sensors to the wooden structure. We measured the existing component, modeled the replacement wheel and supports in CATIA, exported STL files and produced the parts by 3D printing.

Acquiring brake and weight-shift measurements

The sensing architecture combines two incremental rotary encoders for the brake handles with two load cells located around the harness. The latter replaced an accelerometer so that the simulator could react more directly to a left–right transfer of the pilot's weight.

The report identifies CZL301 load cells and HX711 amplifier/ADC modules. Each HX711 converts a small load-cell signal into digital readings that the STM32 acquires through clock and data GPIO signals.

Load-cell calibration
m = (xraw − xtare) / kscale

The firmware subtracts a zero-load offset and divides by a calibration factor. The result is expressed in grams only if the scale factor has been calibrated accordingly.

At startup, the firmware averages 20 raw samples to tare each HX711. During acquisition, it averages three readings per sensor to reduce noise. The report also describes an analog low-pass filter associated with the encoder setup.

Embedded processing on the STM32

The firmware uses TIM3 and TIM4 in encoder mode to track the two handle positions, TIM2 as a microsecond time base, GPIO bit-banging for the HX711 modules, and two UART interfaces: one for debugging and one for application data.

To avoid sudden jumps when the 16-bit hardware counters wrap, the encoder code initializes them near the midpoint (32,767), computes signed count differences, and accumulates motion into 32-bit software positions.

Encoder position accumulation
pk = pk−1 + Δck

Here Δck is the signed difference between successive 16-bit counter readings, interpreted with wraparound handling.

The main loop performs sensor acquisition and updates the control information at a reported interval of approximately 20–30 ms. The original firmware description refers to a combined value called SendValue; the communication chapter also documents left and right command percentages. Both are part of the report, but it does not fully reconcile the two representations.

Sending commands wirelessly to the PC

A wireless link was important to avoid restricting the pilot's movement. The team compared an ESP8266 Wi-Fi module with the HC-05 Bluetooth module, then selected the HC-05 for its straightforward UART integration and adequate throughput.

Early connection tests were unreliable, with successful connections reported only about one time in three. The module was subsequently configured using AT commands to operate in master mode, after which the report describes the connection as stable. The UART configuration was 9,600 baud, 8N1.

Brake-dominant command mixing
u = 0.8ubrake + 0.2uweight

The reported control strategy assigns 80% of steering influence to the brake handles and 20% to weight shifting. The STM32 processes the sensor measurements before sending application-level commands to the PC.

Integrating the physical controller into Unity

Rather than building the entire flight engine from scratch, the team adapted an existing Unity project. Bluetooth reception was integrated into the application's initial menu scene so that the connection could be established before starting a level. The simulator was reorganized into distinct scenes for initialization, level selection, gameplay and results.

Three progressive flight challenges

The first level focuses on basic steering and landing precision, evaluating how close the player lands to a target. The second asks the pilot to find stationary thermal updrafts to gain altitude. The third increases the difficulty by introducing moving thermals that require continuous trajectory adjustments.

The interface displays results at the end of a level and allows the player to retry, advance or return to the main menu. The team also tested the simulator through a VR headset as an additional immersion experiment.

Engineering outcome

This project required integration across several disciplines: mechanical design for reliable encoder mounts, signal acquisition for force and rotary measurements, embedded firmware for processing and calibration, wireless communication for PC connectivity, and interactive software for the flight experience.

The report documents a functional end-to-end architecture and the development of three interactive scenarios. It does not provide a formal end-to-end latency benchmark or quantitative accuracy evaluation, so those performance claims are intentionally not added here.

Engineering takeaway

The key achievement is the integration of physical human inputs into a coherent embedded and interactive system — from custom 3D-printed mechanisms and sensor electronics to real-time control of a Unity simulation.
